title: Hospitality without grumbling (1 Peter 4:7–11)
hookLine: love covers a multitude of sins; use every gift for others
tomorrow: how do you throw a worry that won't let go of you?

cards: A casserole on the porch, foil on top, still warm. Then another. Then the doorbell, again, and a coat to hang, and a chair to find, and somewhere in the kitchen a low mutter starts.
So how do you open your door without the sigh? 1 Peter names that exact moment: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Not only open the door.
Open it without the grumble. And the letter's way there begins with a strange sense of time.

teach.h: THE END IS NEAR: SO, THE TABLE.
teach.b: It opens with urgency: "the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer." You'd expect the next line to be about the sky. It's about the people across the table.
"And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins." Charity is the King James word for love.

Some readers picture a blanket: the faults are still there, but love stops pulling the blanket back to look at them. The line echoes an older proverb: "love covereth all sins." Then the welcome, without grudging.

Then the reason the grumble can go: "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." A steward looks after what belongs to someone else.
The house, the soup, the knack for listening or fixing a sink: none of it started as yours to guard.
And here's the detail to tell a friend: a welcome often speaks before anyone does.
The smell of bread in the oven, coffee on, soup on the stove. A house can say come in, there's enough, before the door is even open. That's hospitality without grumbling, in a smell.

how: Christians practice hospitality by hosting meals, bringing food to families in hard times and welcoming newcomers, and some churches read 1 Peter 4:8–10 when they talk about serving with their gifts.

games.q: your roommate's sister is on your couch for a week. you said yes. by day three you're keeping score of every dish she leaves. what does 1 Peter 4 point you toward?
o: a list of house rules taped to the fridge.
love that covers, and a welcome without grudging.
telling her it's time to go a few days early.
games.why: above all things, fervent charity: love that covers instead of counting, and hospitality without grudging.

practice: Find something with a scent nearby: tea, coffee, an orange peel, bread, even a bar of soap. Breathe it in slowly, a few times, and notice how a smell says welcome before anyone speaks.
On each breath out, let a little of the grumble go with it.

wordCard.voice: Hospitality without grumbling. First Peter, chapter four: welcome one another without grudging, and use every gift as a steward, for others.

orig.note: Greek: love. the word the King James renders 'charity' in 1 Peter 4:8.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: love covers, a blanket over the people at your table, not a spotlight. Rest easy.
